An extended wet period from much of Monday night through Wednesday morning is expected, associated with a slow moving and thermally strong cold front.
Seasonably cool conditions in the middle to end of the week, with a couple shower chances Wednesday, and a more defined system potentially late week into the weekend.

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
305 PM EDT Sat Oct 10 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 305 PM EDT Saturday...

Greater confidence in sharply colder daytime temperatures on 
Tuesday, especially in eastern Vermont and St. Lawrence Valley.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 305 PM EDT Saturday...

1. Rain associated with the remnants of Isaias will bring a 
soaking rainfall Sunday night with no significant impacts for 
our area. 

2. An extended wet period from much of Monday night through 
Wednesday morning is expected, associated with a slow moving and 
thermally strong cold front. 

3. Seasonably cool conditions in the middle to end of the week, 
with a couple shower chances Wednesday, and a more defined system 
potentially late week into the weekend.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 305 PM EDT Saturday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: 

As seasonably strong high pressure (~1030 millibars) moves to our 
southeast tonight, a tightening pressure gradient will develop with 
modest south/southeast flow beneath thickening high altitude clouds. 
Most notably terrain effects will lead to another breezy period 
tomorrow morning on the east side of Lake Champlain in the northern 
portions of the valley, where gusts should exceed 30 MPH for much of 
the day and a Lake Wind Advisory will probably be needed. Otherwise, 
we will await rain overspreading the region from the south as the 
remnants of post-tropical cyclone Isaias move northeastward near the 
Appalachian Mountains. The low track will then be shunted to the 
east across the Mid-Atlantic region Sunday night, but far enough 
north such that plenty of lift and moisture will reach our latitude 
before precipitation gradually exits to our east overnight. 

High confidence of some rain, starting roughly sunset in southern 
portions of the region and towards midnight in northeastern Vermont, 
remains on track. Biggest impact of this rain would probably be 
related to hydroplaning following an extended dry period, but 
overall it should be a beneficial rainfall. Most guidance shows a 
relatively short duration of lighter rain towards the International 
Border where PoPs are somewhat lower on an hourly basis, but think 
at least some rain will occur. Generally greater rainfall amounts 
are more likely as you go southward with this event given the storm 
track. However, strong mid-level frontogenesis will help produce 
strips of heavier rainfall oriented from west to east, which are 
always difficult to pin down. Rainfall rates for at least a few 
hours will increase within these bands, likely 0.1-0.2" an hour, 
well shy of truly heavy rain. As such, localized pockets of heavier 
rain can be expected; think the 90th percentile amounts in the 1 to 
1.5" range look reasonable as a reasonable high end amount which 
still would not produce any hazardous hydrological conditions. That 
said, the deterministic forecast is fairly close to the REFS 
probability matched mean with more modest amounts; most likely storm 
totals in our northernmost counties are less than 0.1" while 
reaching about 0.5"-0.75" in Rutland and Windsor counties; most 
areas in between will vary widely between 0.1"-0.5". Most likely 
end time of rain in most locations is during the Monday morning
hours roughly from 2 to 5 AM in northernmost Vermont and 
northern New York and 5 to 8 AM in the rest of Vermont. A very 
narrow ridge will follow ahead our next weather system providing
mainly dry conditions during the day Monday, aside from 
localized showers/drizzle in the mountains with lingering 
moisture possibly trapped below an inversion around 2 to 3 
thousand feet elevation. Valley locations will probably see 
their warmest day of the week as a result.

KEY MESSAGE 2: Following the rain on Sunday night, another high 
probability rainfall event (about 100% chance of rain) continues to 
be expected for Tuesday. Moisture from the remnants of Tropical 
Storm Rachel in the eastern Pacific will be carried out ahead of a 
strengthening front approaching from the north while high pressure 
builds in across eastern Canada, producing a cold air damming setup 
for New England. 

Rainfall amounts could be rather substantial, with high 
statistical confidence of totals from Tuesday through Tuesday 
night exceeding 0.5" for nearly all of our region, and even 1" 
probabilities are in the 50-70% range in much of northern New 
York and northern portions of Vermont. While the setup for 
widespread rain with this boundary stalling out while a wave of 
low pressure passing through our region is largely in good 
agreement, the position of this system is highly uncertain. 

Even with a relatively short lead time (day 4), there is very 
large spread in the upper air pattern and associated position of
boundaries that lead to important differences in our sensible 
weather. The GFS and most of its ensemble members have lower 
heights upstream, leading to a low pressure track farther north 
and warmer/more unstable air moving through our region. 
Meanwhile, the ECMWF and many of its ensemble members, RRFS, and
NAM12 show a pronounced cold air damming scenario as shallow 
cold air gets locked in across the St. Lawrence Valley and 
eastern/northeastern Vermont. This scenario, in which low 
pressure would be delayed and pass overhead or even south of our
region, would lead to an all day rain event. The aforementioned
areas would be quite chilly with temperatures holding in the 
mid 40s to near 50, while south/southeast winds in the Champlain
Valley and Adirondacks transport deep moisture and maintain 
somewhat milder air. We have trended temperatures this way given
the consensus; note there is some merit in the GFS depiction, 
so the forecast remains unusually uncertain and we can expect 
non-diurnal temperature fluctuations. 

KEY MESSAGE 3: As our Tuesday system departs, decent caa will filter 
seasonably cool air into the region from the northwest. Wrap around 
moisture Wednesday associated with cooling aloft, will likely lead 
to some shallow instability showers across the region. Isolated to 
scattered showers will be possible, especially in the Northeast 
Kingdom and Adirondacks. Expectations will likely follow breaks of 
sun followed by a quick shower. PoPs will likely see increases in 
the coming days as we get closer to mid week. Winds will also be 
seasonably breezy with some channeled winds anticipated Wednesday. 
Brisk breezy northwest winds can be expected. Temperatures will drop 
slightly Wednesday into Thursday as weak ridging builds into the 
region. Highs on Wednesday and Thursday will be in the low to mid 
50s, with possible near 60s in southern Vermont depending on cloud 
coverage. Lows Wednesday and Thursday night will dip into the low to 
mid 30s areawide with some upper 20s across the Adirondacks. 

The pattern then becomes quite varied amongst the global models. 
There is good agreement in some sunshine Thursday, however, the 
arrival of our next system remains in question. Model timing and 
handling of a closed low in the Intermountain West is leading to 
start difference between the GFS and Euro ensembles for 
precipitation chances late next week into the weekend. Regardless, 
there does look to be good chances for rain this weekend, but the 
timing of the system is still uncertain. Additionally, regardless of 
the timing, as our late week system arrives, a strong 50-60 knot jet 
looks to be tied to the system which will bring chances for gusty 
winds, especially for the Champlain and St. Lawrence Valley. GEFS 
and Euro ensemble probabilities of gusts exceeding 25 MPH for most 
locations is between 40-60% Friday into Saturday with probabilities 
of gusts exceeding 35 MPH between 10-30% for the St. Lawrence and 
northern Champlain Valleys.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z SATURDAY THROUGH THURSDAY/...
Through 18Z Sunday...All terminals are expected to remain VFR through
the entire TAF period. Light north-northwesterly winds, mainly 10
knots or less, will continue through sunset. A few isolated gusts
around 15 kts will be possible at BTV this afternoon, but should not
be prevailing. A subtle lake breeze is also ongoing at PBG, but
should go back to prevailing northerly or variable in the next few
hours. Winds will then weaken and turn to the south to southwest
between 00- 06Z for all terminals and begin to increase in magnitude
thereafter as a low level jet at 2000ft agl moves across the area.
LLWS may be present at times, but prevailing LLWS confidence is low
at this time, and not included in this TAF package. As winds turn to
the south, winds will increase back to 10-15 knots between 06-12Z
for all terminals. At BTV/PBG/MSS winds will continue to increase
into the late morning with channeled south flow to 15-20 MPH with a
few gusts increasing towards 25 MPH by the end of the TAF period.
SLK, will see similar more elevated winds around 15 knots, though
sheltering should keep the higher gusts more limited. With surface
winds increasing overnight, any chances for fog tonight should be
precluded. Skies will remain clear through the next 6 hours with
some high clouds building from the south this evening and overnight.

Outlook...

Sunday Night: Mainly VFR, with local IFR possible. Chance SHRA.
Columbus Day: Mainly MVFR, with local VFR possible. Slight chance
SHRA.
Monday Night: Mainly MVFR, with local IFR possible. Definite
SHRA.
Tuesday: Mainly MVFR, with areas VFR possible. Definite SHRA.
Tuesday Night: Mainly MVFR, with areas IFR possible. Chance SHRA.
Wednesday: Mainly MVFR, with local IFR possible. Slight chance
SHRA.
Wednesday Night: Mainly MVFR, with local VFR possible. NO SIG WX.
Thursday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
